# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Municipal air quality screening can identify widespread concern while providing limited spatial discrimination for control planning. This study examines whether relative concentration patterns and source contributions add useful information to attainment-oriented screening in Congonhas, a mining-influenced municipality in southeastern Brazil. AERMOD outputs for 2021–2023, driven by a 2023 emissions inventory, were analysed at 1,008 municipal receptors from a regional network of 1,497 locations. Annual means and annual daily P98 indicators were retained separately from regulatory interpretation. Receptor-based quintiles, clustering, spatial correlograms and local Moran statistics were compared before results were linked to 311 municipal zoning records using clipped Voronoi support. Global Moran statistics for log-transformed annual concentrations were 0.662 for PM~10~ and 0.754 for PM~2.5~. Conditional local permutation tests with false-discovery adjustment identified 151 and 126 high–high receptors, respectively. Ward clustering with two groups achieved the highest internal silhouette among the tested alternatives, 0.533, although neighbourhood sensitivity affected local boundaries. Spatially blocked emission–concentration screening produced useful but incomplete predictive associations and did not identify a universal allowable emission threshold. The analysis also identified near-zero-area zoning fragments requiring cadastral review. Relative regionalization exposed patterns obscured by widespread benchmark exceedance, but neither corrected model bias nor demonstrated ambient attainment. Its management value lies in connecting explicit spatial uncertainty, received contributions and within-zone heterogeneity to targeted source investigation and subsequent control scenarios.

Keywords regionalization, spatial autocorrelation, source attribution, land-use planning, mining.
